topic.title: Upper and lower bounds in subtraction and division (applying bounds)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One item in almost every M4 paper, sitting at Q13–Q17 of 21–24 questions. Three marks when the bounds go straight into a given formula (Summer 2024 Q16, h = u² ÷ 2a; November 2024 Q16, S = V² ÷ 2g; Summer 2026 Q14, F = ma rearranged for a). Four marks when a second stage is bolted on: a time in hours and minutes (Summer 2023 Q15), a whole-number count (Summer 2025 Q13) or Pythagoras (November 2025 Q17). Schemes are short MA1 chains with an A1 on the final value, and that A mark wants the untruncated calculator display.
mustMemorise: Half unit = half of the rounding unit: nearest 5 → 2.5, nearest 50 → 25, nearest 2 → 1, nearest 0.5 → 0.25, 1 d.p. → 0.05, 3 s.f. of 4.68 → 0.005
Greatest a − b = UB(a) − LB(b); least a − b = LB(a) − UB(b)
Greatest a ÷ b = UB(a) ÷ LB(b); least a ÷ b = LB(a) ÷ UB(b)
Bound the inputs, never the answer: substitute once, then leave the full calculator display
Change minutes into decimal hours by dividing by 60 before you bound the time
A greatest possible whole-number count is rounded down, not up
A suitable degree of accuracy is the most figures on which the two bounds agree
onFormulaSheet: Volume of a prism, volume and surface area of a sphere and a cone, area of a trapezium — the only formulae a bounds item can borrow from the Higher sheet
No bounds rule of any kind is printed: the half-unit rule and the max/min pairings are memory
notOnThisSpec: Error-interval notation such as 47.5 ≤ m < 52.5: no CCEA Mathematics statement mentions error intervals, and every M4 bounds item read asks for a maximum, a minimum or a named bound as a value (Summer 2023 Q15, Summer 2024 Q16, November 2024 Q16, Summer 2025 Q13, November 2025 Q17, Summer 2026 Q14)
Bounds of an addition or a multiplication on their own — that is M3-NA-03 and it is assumed here
Percentage error, absolute error and relative error: these words appear in no statement of the CCEA Mathematics specification

Truncated values: the word truncate appears in no CCEA Mathematics paper in the corpus, and every item says correct to. The truncation rule is here because a given degree of accuracy admits it and it costs one sentence, not because CCEA has asked for it

note.title: Upper and lower bounds in subtraction and division
note.subject: maths

given: Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length
Area of a trapezium = ½(a + b)h
Volume of a sphere, surface area of a sphere, volume of a cone, curved surface area of a cone
mustKnow: Half unit = half of the rounding unit; the bounds are the stated value ± the half unit
Greatest a − b = UB(a) − LB(b); least a − b = LB(a) − UB(b)
Greatest a ÷ b = UB(a) ÷ LB(b); least a ÷ b = LB(a) ÷ UB(b)
Speed = distance ÷ time and density = mass ÷ volume are not on the sheet
Pythagoras' theorem a² + b² = c² is not on the sheet; nor is the area of a circle πr²

notOnThisSpec: Error-interval notation such as 47.5 ≤ m < 52.5: no CCEA Mathematics statement mentions error intervals, and every M4 bounds item read asks for a maximum, a minimum or a named bound as a value (Summer 2023 Q15, Summer 2024 Q16, November 2024 Q16, Summer 2025 Q13, November 2025 Q17, Summer 2026 Q14)
Bounds of an addition or a multiplication on their own — that is M3-NA-03 and it is assumed here
Percentage error, absolute error and relative error: these words appear in no statement of the CCEA Mathematics specification

Truncated values: the word truncate appears in no CCEA Mathematics paper in the corpus, and every item says correct to. The truncation rule is here because a given degree of accuracy admits it and it costs one sentence, not because CCEA has asked for it

mustBeAbleTo: Write the half unit for any stated accuracy — nearest 5, nearest 50, nearest 2, nearest 0.5, 1 d.p., 2 or 3 significant figures — and then the two bounds
Write the interval of a truncated value as from the stated value up to but not including the next unit
Find the greatest and least possible value of a difference by pairing an upper bound with a lower bound
Find the greatest and least possible value of a quotient by dividing an upper bound by a lower bound, and the reverse
Substitute bounds into a formula such as h = u² ÷ 2a, squaring the bound of u and doubling the bound of a
Convert a time in hours and minutes into decimal hours before bounding it, then find a maximum or minimum average speed
Find a greatest possible whole-number count and round it down, giving an integer
Find the greatest possible area left when one shape is removed from another, by taking the upper bound of the whole and the lower bound of the part
Choose a suitable degree of accuracy by rounding both bounds and keeping the figures on which they agree
Leave the full calculator display when the question asks for a bound, and round only when an accuracy is stated
sheet.howExamined: M4 (Higher, calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks, 21–24 questions). One bounds item per paper at Q13–Q17. Three marks when the bounds go into a printed formula: Summer 2024 Q16 (h = u² ÷ 2a, answer 23.36456538), November 2024 Q16 (S = V² ÷ 2g, answer 10.35504844), Summer 2026 Q14 (F = ma, minimum acceleration, answer in m/s²). Four marks when a second stage is added: Summer 2023 Q15 (maximum average speed from 62 km and 1 hour 11 minutes, answer 53.19148936), Summer 2025 Q13 (greatest number of containers from masses to the nearest 5 kg and the nearest 100 kg, answer 32), November 2025 Q17 (upper bound of the third side of a right-angled triangle, answer 3.863512003). The schemes are MA1 chains — one mark for the bounds identified, one for the substitution, an A1 for the value — and the value printed in the scheme is the full display, so a rounded answer risks the A mark unless the question states an accuracy. Command words: Calculate, Find, Work out, Write down, with greatest possible, least possible, maximum and minimum doing the work in the stem.
traps: Halving the wrong thing: 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg has bounds 47.5 and 52.5, not 45 and 55 — the single commonest loss on this topic (Summer 2025 M4 Q13)
Leaving a count of whole objects as a decimal, or rounding it up: a greatest possible number of items rounds down (Summer 2025 M4 Q13)
Bounding the answer instead of the inputs: calculating with the given values and then adding a half unit to the result (November 2025 M4 Q17, where about 30% scored full marks)
Pairing two upper bounds in a subtraction or a division, when one upper and one lower is what makes the result largest (November 2025 M4 Q17)
Treating 1 hour 11 minutes as 1.11 hours, or bounding 71 minutes and then forgetting to divide by 60 (Summer 2023 M4 Q15)
Reading the formula loosely: u not squared, a not doubled (Summer 2024 M4 Q16 and November 2024 M4 Q16, where the bounds themselves were usually right)
Rounding the bound: the scheme prints 3.863512003 and 53.19148936, so leave the display unless an accuracy is demanded (November 2025 M4 Q17, Summer 2023 M4 Q15)
Naming a degree of accuracy without checking it: 2.7158… and 2.6757… agree at 2.7 to 2 significant figures and disagree at 3, so 2 significant figures is the honest answer

workedExamples.stem:
A shelf has an internal width of $96$ cm, correct to the nearest centimetre. A row of box files standing on it has a total width of $91.5$ cm, correct to the nearest $0.5$ cm.

Find the greatest possible gap left on the shelf, and the least possible gap.

steps.working: Shelf: half unit $= 0.5$, so $95.5 \le w < 96.5$. Files: half unit $= 0.25$, so $91.25 \le f < 91.75$.
steps.decision: The half unit is half of the rounding unit, and the rounding unit is whatever the question names. Nearest centimetre halves to 0.5; nearest 0.5 cm halves to 0.25. I write all four bounds before I write anything else, because every later choice is a choice between them.

options: 0.25, because the rounding unit is 0.5 cm and half of 0.5 is 0.25
0.5, because measurements are always bounded by half a centimetre
0.05, because 91.5 is given to one decimal place
whyMenu.explain: The stem names the rounding unit, not the number of decimal places. Nearest 0.5 cm gives a half unit of 0.25 cm.

steps.decision: I write the calculation in symbols first. The gap is a subtraction, so the two quantities pull in opposite directions: whatever makes the shelf larger makes the gap larger, and whatever makes the files larger makes the gap smaller.
Widest possible shelf, narrowest possible files. Upper bound minus lower bound. This is the pairing the November 2025 examiners said candidates reversed.
The mirror image: narrowest shelf, widest files. Lower bound minus upper bound. Neither answer uses 96 or 91.5 anywhere.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Greatest gap $5.25$ cm, least gap $3.75$ cm

twin.stem: A doorway is $78$ cm wide, correct to the nearest centimetre. A wardrobe is $76.5$ cm wide, correct to the nearest $0.5$ cm. Find the greatest possible clearance when the wardrobe is carried through.

workedExamples.stem:
A sandbag has a mass of $35$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg. The safe working load of a hoist is $900$ kg, correct to the nearest $50$ kg.

Work out the greatest possible number of sandbags the hoist can lift.

steps.decision: Half of 5 is 2.5. This one line is where Summer 2025 was lost: candidates wrote 30 and 40 because they subtracted and added the whole 5 instead of half of it.

options: 32.5 kg, because half of 5 kg is 2.5 kg
30 kg, because the next multiple of 5 below 35 is 30
34.5 kg, because 35 is a whole number so the half unit is 0.5
whyMenu.explain: Anything from 32.5 kg up to 37.5 kg rounds to 35 kg when you round to the nearest 5 kg, so 32.5 is the lower bound.

steps.decision: Half of 50 is 25. Same rule, larger unit; nothing about the method changes.

steps.working: Number of bags $=$ load $\div$ mass of one bag, so greatest $= 925 \div 32.5$
steps.decision: A division, so the pairing is an upper over a lower. Heaviest possible allowance, lightest possible bag: both push the count up.
I keep the display. Rounding here to 28.5 or 28.46 would be the rounded-display slip the reports name every series.

A count of bags is a whole number, and 29 bags would weigh at least $29 \times 32.5 = 942.5$ kg, which is more than 925 kg. So the decimal is rounded down, not up: 28 bags weigh at least 910 kg, which the hoist can take.

options: 28, because 29 bags would need at least 942.5 kg of allowance
28.5, because the answer should be given to one decimal place
whyMenu.explain: A greatest possible count is rounded down: the 29th bag does not fit under any allowed load. Leaving a decimal scores nothing for the final mark.

twin.stem: A paving slab has a mass of $18$ kg, correct to the nearest $2$ kg. A trolley is rated to carry $260$ kg, correct to the nearest $20$ kg. Work out the greatest possible number of slabs the trolley can carry.

workedExamples.stem:
A train travels $87$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre. The journey takes $1$ hour $24$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute.

Calculate the maximum average speed of the train in km/h.

steps.working: Distance: $86.5 \le d < 87.5$, so the upper bound is $87.5$ km.
steps.decision: Nearest kilometre, half unit 0.5. Speed is distance divided by time, so the largest speed wants the largest distance.

steps.working: $1$ h $24$ min $= 84$ minutes, so $83.5 \le t < 84.5$ minutes.
steps.decision: I turn the time into one unit before I bound it. The accuracy is to the nearest minute, so the half unit is half a minute — and it is half a minute of the total, 84 minutes, not of the 24.

steps.working: Minimum time $= 83.5 \div 60 = 1.4166\ldots$ h, keeping the display.
steps.decision: km/h needs hours. Minutes divided by 60 gives decimal hours. Writing 1 h 23.5 min as 1.235 h is the slip the Summer 2023 report singled out, and it is not a small one: it changes the answer by about 12 km/h.

options: $1.235$ h, because 1 h 23.5 min reads as 1.235
$1.235$ h, because 23.5 minutes is 0.235 of an hour
whyMenu.explain: Minutes are sixtieths, not hundredths or thousandths. Divide the whole time in minutes by 60.

steps.decision: Largest distance over smallest time. I use the stored value, not 1.42, so the display is the answer the scheme prints. Equivalently $87.5 \times 60 \div 83.5$.

twin.stem: A ferry crosses $54$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre, in $2$ hours $18$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. Calculate the maximum average speed in km/h.

workedExamples.stem:
A ball bearing rolls down a ramp and stops after a distance $s$ metres, where

$s = \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$

$v = 5.82$ m/s, correct to $3$ significant figures.
$a = 3.6$ m/s$^2$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of $s$. Leave the full calculator display.

steps.working: $v$: last significant figure is the hundredths, half unit $0.005$, so $5.815 \le v < 5.825$.
steps.decision: Three significant figures in 5.82 means the 2 is the last one, in the hundredths column, so the half unit is 0.005. Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit, and the half unit belongs to the place value of the last one.

steps.working: $a$: one decimal place, half unit $0.05$, so $3.55 \le a < 3.65$.
steps.decision: Half of 0.1 is 0.05. All four bounds are now on the page.

steps.working: $s$ largest when $v$ is largest and $a$ is smallest: $s_{\max} = \dfrac{5.825^2}{2 \times 3.55}$
steps.decision: $v$ is on the top, so the biggest $v$ gives the biggest $s$. $a$ is on the bottom, so the smallest $a$ gives the biggest $s$. The formula is read symbol by symbol: $v$ is squared and $a$ is doubled. Summer 2024 and November 2024 both report that the bounds were right and the formula was not.

options: $\dfrac{5.825^2}{3.55}$, because the 2 belongs to the square
$\dfrac{5.825}{2 \times 3.55}$, because the square applies to the whole fraction
whyMenu.explain: The 2 multiplies $a$ and the square sits on $v$ only. Both slips are named in the November 2024 report.

steps.decision: I write both intermediate values in full. No rounding: 33.93 and 7.1 would already cost accuracy in the final figure.
The display is the answer. Substituting the given values would have produced 4.7045, which is not an upper bound of anything.

twin.stem: For the same formula $s = \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$, take $v = 7.64$ m/s correct to $3$ significant figures and $a = 2.5$ m/s$^2$ correct to $1$ decimal place. Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of $s$.

items.stem: A crate has a mass of $60$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg. What is the lower bound of its mass?
items.skill: Half unit for a rounding unit larger than 1

options.feedback: Half of 5 is 2.5, so anything from 57.5 kg up to 62.5 kg rounds to 60 kg. The lower bound is 57.5 kg.
The whole 5 was subtracted instead of half of it. A mass of 56 kg would round to 55 kg, not 60 kg, so 55 is too low. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 turned on exactly this line.
That is the half unit for the nearest whole kilogram. The stem says nearest 5 kg, so halve the 5, not the 1.

items.stem: A length is $4.68$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures. What is its upper bound?

options.feedback: The third significant figure is the 8, in the hundredths column, so the half unit is 0.005 and the upper bound is 4.685 cm. This is the bound November 2025 M4 Q17 needed.
A whole unit of the last place was added rather than half of it. 4.687 would still round to 4.69, so 4.69 is not the boundary.
That is the bound for 2 significant figures. Count the significant figures in the value you were given: 4, 6 and 8 are three of them.

items.stem: A timer shows $12.4$ s. It does not round: it cuts the display off at $1$ decimal place. Which interval holds the true time $t$?

options.feedback: Cutting off, or truncating, keeps everything from 12.4 up to but not including 12.5. The stated value is itself the lower bound.
That is the interval for a value rounded to 1 decimal place. A display that cuts off can never be above the true value, so nothing below 12.4 is possible.
The interval runs upwards from the shown value, not downwards: a truncated display is the true value with the extra digits thrown away.

items.stem: $a = 9.2$ correct to $1$ decimal place and $b = 3.74$ correct to $2$ decimal places. What is the greatest possible value of $a - b$?

options.feedback: Upper bound of $a$ minus lower bound of $b$: $9.25 - 3.735 = 5.515$. Take the most and remove the least.
Both upper bounds were used: $9.25 - 3.745$. Subtracting a larger number makes the answer smaller, so this is not the maximum.
That is $9.2 - 3.74$, the given values. A bounds question never uses them; they are the middle of each interval.

items.stem: $p = 46$ correct to the nearest whole number and $q = 5.2$ correct to $1$ decimal place. What is the greatest possible value of $p \div q$, to $3$ decimal places?

options.feedback: $46.5 \div 5.15 = 9.029126\ldots$ Biggest top, smallest bottom.
Both upper bounds were used: $46.5 \div 5.25$. Dividing by a larger number makes the answer smaller, so this is below the maximum.
That is $46 \div 5.2$, the given values. The bounds have to go in before you divide.

items.stem: A journey takes $1$ hour $36$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. What is the shortest possible time, in hours?
items.skill: Bounding a time given in hours and minutes

options.feedback: $1$ h $36$ min $= 96$ min, so the lower bound is $95.5$ min, and $95.5 \div 60 = 1.591666\ldots$ h.
1 h 35.5 min has been read as the decimal 1.355. Minutes are sixtieths: change the whole time to minutes, bound it, then divide by 60. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was lost here.
That is the given time, $96 \div 60$, with no bound applied. The shortest possible time is half a minute less.

items.stem: You are asked for the upper bound of a calculation. What do you do first?
items.skill: Bound the inputs, not the answer

options.text: Replace each given value by the bound that makes the result largest, then calculate once.
options.feedback: Bounds go in at the start. One substitution, one calculation, and the display is the bound. Full-mark answers in November 2025 listed all four bounds first.

options.text: Calculate with the given values, then add half a unit to the answer.
options.feedback: Half units do not survive a calculation: squaring, dividing and square-rooting all change them. About 30% reached full marks on November 2025 M4 Q17 and this was the main reason.

options.text: Calculate with the given values, then round the answer up.
options.feedback: Rounding up is not the same as an upper bound. The upper bound comes from the inputs, and it is usually nowhere near the rounded-up value.

items.stem: A length has lower bound $6.0473\ldots$ m and upper bound $6.0518\ldots$ m. What is the length to a suitable degree of accuracy?
items.skill: Choosing a degree of accuracy from the bounds

options.feedback: Round both bounds: to 3 significant figures both give 6.05, so 6.05 m is safe. To 4 significant figures they give 6.047 and 6.052, which disagree, so stop at three.
Only the lower bound was rounded. The upper bound gives 6.052 to the same accuracy, so the fourth figure is not known and cannot be quoted.
A midpoint is a guess dressed up as precision. A suitable degree of accuracy is the figures on which the two bounds actually agree.

parts.stem:
A plank is $84$ cm long, correct to the nearest centimetre.

Write down the **lower bound** of its length.
hints: Half of 1 cm is 0.5 cm.
Take the half unit away from 84.
parts.workedSolution: Nearest centimetre, so the half unit is $0.5$ cm. Lower bound $= 84 - 0.5 = 83.5$ cm.

parts.stem:
A parcel has a mass of $2.6$ kg, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Write down the **upper bound** of its mass.
hints: One decimal place means the rounding unit is 0.1.
Half of 0.1 is 0.05.
parts.workedSolution: One decimal place, so the half unit is $0.05$ kg. Upper bound $= 2.6 + 0.05 = 2.65$ kg.

parts.stem:
A kettlebell has a mass of $45$ kg, correct to the **nearest 5 kg**.

Write down the lower bound of its mass.
hints: Halve the rounding unit, not the number.
Half of 5 is 2.5.
parts.workedSolution: The rounding unit is $5$ kg, so the half unit is $2.5$ kg. Lower bound $= 45 - 2.5 = 42.5$ kg.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole 5 kg was taken off instead of half of it. Anything from 42.5 kg upwards rounds to 45 kg, so 42.5 is the boundary. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 was decided on this line.

parts.stem:
The attendance at a match is reported as $3400$, correct to **2 significant figures**.

Write down the upper bound of the attendance.
hints: The second significant figure is the 4, in the hundreds column.
Half of 100 is 50.
parts.workedSolution: Two significant figures makes the $4$ the last one, so the rounding unit is $100$ and the half unit is $50$. Upper bound $= 3400 + 50 = 3450$.

commonErrors.feedback: The half unit was taken from the units column. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit: here the last significant figure is the 4, worth 400, so the rounding unit is 100.

parts.stem:
A stopwatch does not round: it **cuts the display off** at $1$ decimal place. It shows $9.4$ s.

Write down the upper bound of the true time.
hints: A display that cuts off can never show more than the true time.
What is the next value the display would show?
parts.workedSolution: Truncating keeps every time from $9.4$ s up to, but not including, $9.5$ s: $9.4 \le t < 9.5$. The upper bound is $9.5$ s, and it is not reached.

commonErrors.feedback: The half-unit rule was applied to a value that was not rounded. A truncated display is never above the true time, so the interval runs upwards from 9.4, not either side of it.

parts.stem:
$a = 14.7$ correct to $1$ decimal place and $b = 8.24$ correct to $2$ decimal places.

Work out the **greatest possible** value of $a - b$.
hints: Write all four bounds first: 14.65, 14.75, 8.235, 8.245.
To take away as little as possible, use the lower bound of $b$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both upper bounds were used. Taking away a bigger number leaves less, so the maximum needs the lower bound of $b$. The method mark is for the pairing 14.75 with 8.235.

parts.stem:
$a = 14.7$ correct to $1$ decimal place and $b = 8.24$ correct to $2$ decimal places.

Work out the **least possible** value of $a - b$.
hints: The minimum is the mirror image of the maximum.
Smallest $a$, largest $b$.
parts.workedSolution: Least $a - b = 14.65 - 8.245 = 6.405$. Note that neither answer uses $14.7$ or $8.24$.

commonErrors.feedback: Two lower bounds were used. For the least difference the number being taken away must be as large as possible: $14.65 - 8.245$.

parts.stem:
$p = 46$ correct to the nearest whole number and $q = 5.2$ correct to $1$ decimal place.

From those bounds, work out the **greatest possible** value of $p \div q$. Leave the full calculator display.
hints: Dividing by a smaller number gives a larger answer.
parts.workedSolution: Greatest $p \div q = 46.5 \div 5.15 = 9.029126213\ldots$ The biggest top and the smallest bottom both push the quotient up.

commonErrors.feedback: $46.5 \div 5.25$ uses both upper bounds. A division reverses the effect of the bottom: to make the answer as large as possible the divisor must be as small as possible.

parts.stem:
$p = 46$ correct to the nearest whole number and $q = 5.2$ correct to $1$ decimal place.

From those bounds, work out the **least possible** value of $p \div q$.
hints: Smallest top, largest bottom.
parts.workedSolution: Least $p \div q = 45.5 \div 5.25 = 8.666666\ldots$

parts.stem:
A lorry covers $315$ km, correct to the **nearest 5 km**, in $4.2$ hours, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Calculate the maximum possible average speed of the lorry.

Give your answer to $3$ **significant figures**.

scheme.for: 76.5, from 76.50602410; the full display is also accepted

hints: Half of 5 km is 2.5 km; half of 0.1 h is 0.05 h.
Speed = distance ÷ time, so the maximum wants the furthest distance in the shortest time.
The stem states 3 significant figures, so round once, at the very end.
parts.workedSolution: Distance: $312.5 \le d < 317.5$. Time: $4.15 \le t < 4.25$. Maximum speed $= 317.5 \div 4.15 = 76.50602409\ldots$ km/h, which is $76.5$ km/h to $3$ significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: 320 was used as the upper bound of the distance, which is the whole 5 km added instead of 2.5 km. The bound is 317.5 km.
$315 \div 4.2$ uses the given values, so it is neither a maximum nor a minimum. Substitute the bounds before you divide.

context.setting: A sample of alloy weighed and measured in a school laboratory

parts.stem:
A sample of alloy has a mass of $63.4$ g, correct to $1$ decimal place, and a volume of $8.5$ cm$^3$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Calculate the minimum possible density of the alloy. Give your answer **with its units**.

scheme.for: 7.409356725 g/cm³ (accept the full display or 7.41); the unit is required because the question asks for it

hints: Density = mass ÷ volume, and it is not on the formula sheet.
The smallest density comes from the smallest mass in the largest volume.

commonErrors.feedback: $63.45 \div 8.45$ is the maximum, not the minimum. For the smallest density, take the least mass and spread it through the largest volume.

context.setting: A projectile formula used in a physics class

parts.stem:
The greatest height $h$ metres reached by a ball thrown straight up is given by

$h = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

$u = 13.7$ m/s, correct to $1$ decimal place.
$g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Using those bounds, calculate the **upper bound** of $h$.
hints: $u$ is on the top, so the largest $u$ gives the largest $h$; $g$ is on the bottom, so the smallest $g$ gives the largest $h$.
Square the bound of $u$ and double the bound of $g$.

commonErrors.feedback: $g$ was not doubled: the calculation was $13.75^2 \div 9.75$. The 2 multiplies $g$, and the bounds were already right, so this is a reading error, not a bounds error. Summer 2024 and November 2024 both name it.
The given values 13.7 and 9.8 were substituted. That is the value of $h$ itself, not its upper bound: the bounds must go in before the calculation.

context.setting: A right-angled triangle with two measured sides

parts.stem:
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $12.8$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place, and one of the shorter sides is $7.35$ cm, correct to $2$ decimal places.

Calculate the **upper bound** of the third side.
hints: Pythagoras' theorem is not on the formula sheet: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, so the third side is $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$.
Under the square root there is a subtraction, so pair the largest hypotenuse with the smallest known side.

commonErrors.feedback: Both upper bounds went under the root. The known side is being taken away, so the smallest one leaves the most: pair 12.85 with 7.345. November 2025 M4 Q17 turned on this pairing.
The third side was found from the given values and then half a unit was added. Half units do not pass through a square root; bound the two sides first, then calculate once.

context.setting: A square cut from a rectangle of plywood

parts.stem:
A rectangle of plywood measures $18.2$ cm by $11.6$ cm, each correct to $1$ decimal place. A square of side $6.4$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place, is cut out of it.

Calculate the **greatest possible** area of plywood left. Give your answer **with its units**.

scheme.for: their rectangle area - their square area
172.29 cm²; the unit is required because the question asks for it

hints: The area left is a subtraction, so the rectangle wants to be as large as possible and the square as small as possible.
Upper bounds of both sides of the rectangle; lower bound of the side of the square.
parts.workedSolution: Greatest area left $= (18.25 \times 11.65) - 6.35^2 = 212.6125 - 40.3225 = 172.29$ cm$^2$. Both sides of the rectangle take their upper bound because the area is a product, and the square takes its lower bound because it is being removed.

commonErrors.feedback: The square was given its upper bound as well: $212.6125 - 6.45^2$. A larger hole leaves less plywood, so the maximum needs the smallest possible square.

context.setting: A right-angled triangle LMN with two measured sides

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 340 235' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Right-angled triangle LMN with the right angle at M, hypotenuse LN marked 9.36 cm and side LM marked 6.2 cm'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'><path d='M60 40 L60 180 L290 180 Z'/><path d='M60 161 L79 161 L79 180'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='currentColor'><text x='44' y='33'>L</text><text x='42' y='201'>M</text><text x='294' y='201'>N</text><text x='4' y='116'>6.2 cm</text><text x='188' y='98'>9.36 cm</text><text x='60' y='228' font-size='12'>diagram not drawn accurately</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Right-angled triangle LMN. The right angle is at M. The hypotenuse LN is marked 9.36 cm and the side LM is marked 6.2 cm. The side MN is not marked. Diagram not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
In triangle $LMN$ the angle at $M$ is a right angle.

$LN = 9.36$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures.
$LM = 6.2$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place.

Write down the bound of $LN$ and the bound of $LM$ that make $MN$ as large as possible.
hints: Three significant figures in 9.36 puts the last one in the hundredths, so the half unit is 0.005.
$MN^2 = LN^2 - LM^2$, and $LM$ is the one being taken away.
parts.workedSolution: $LN$: half unit $0.005$, so the upper bound is $9.365$ cm. $LM$: half unit $0.05$, so the lower bound is $6.15$ cm. $MN$ is largest when the hypotenuse is largest and the side removed is smallest.

commonErrors.feedback: The upper bound of $LM$ was chosen. Inside $LN^2 - LM^2$ the term $LM^2$ is subtracted, so a smaller $LM$ leaves a bigger answer. This is the pairing November 2025 candidates reversed.

parts.stem:
Calculate the upper bound of $MN$.

Leave the **full calculator display**.

scheme.for: 7.062628760 (the full display; accept 7.06 only if an accuracy had been stated)

hints: $MN = \sqrt{LN^2 - LM^2}$.
Square each bound before you subtract.
parts.workedSolution: $MN_{\max} = \sqrt{9.365^2 - 6.15^2} = \sqrt{87.703225 - 37.8225} = \sqrt{49.880725} = 7.062628759\ldots$ cm. Nothing is rounded on the way, and the display is what goes on the answer line.

commonErrors.feedback: $MN$ was found from $9.36$ and $6.2$ first and half a unit was added afterwards. Squaring and square-rooting do not carry a half unit through; about 30% of candidates reached full marks in November 2025 and this was the main loss.
The bound was rounded with no accuracy asked for. The scheme prints the long value, so leave the display; a rounded figure risks the accuracy mark.

parts.stem: Explain why the lower bound of $LM$, and not its upper bound, is used in part (b).

accepted: MN squared is LN squared minus LM squared, so taking away a smaller LM leaves a larger MN.
LM is subtracted, so the smallest LM gives the greatest MN.

reject: because lower bounds are always used

scheme.for: states that LM squared is subtracted, so a smaller LM leaves a larger MN
accept: it is being taken away so the least value leaves the most
reject: because it is the lower bound

hints: Look at where $LM$ sits in $LN^2 - LM^2$.
Say what taking away less does to the answer.
parts.workedSolution: $MN^2 = LN^2 - LM^2$, so $LM^2$ is subtracted. Taking away as little as possible leaves as much as possible, which is why $MN$ is largest when $LM$ is at its lower bound.

commonErrors.feedback: Naming the bound is not a reason. The mark is for saying that $LM^2$ is subtracted, so the smallest $LM$ leaves the largest $MN$.

context.setting: A cyclist's timed ride between two towns

parts.stem:
A cyclist rides $41$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre. The ride takes $1$ hour $52$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute.

Work out the **shortest possible** time for the ride, in hours.

scheme.for: 112 minutes seen and 111.5 as the lower bound

hints: Turn the whole time into minutes first: $1$ h $52$ min $= 112$ min.
Nearest minute, so the half unit is half a minute.
Divide by 60 to get decimal hours.
parts.workedSolution: $1$ h $52$ min $= 112$ minutes, so $111.5 \le t < 112.5$ minutes. In hours the shortest possible time is $111.5 \div 60 = 1.858333333\ldots$ h.

commonErrors.feedback: $1$ h $51.5$ min has been written as the decimal $1.515$. Minutes are sixtieths of an hour, so convert the whole time to minutes, bound it, then divide by 60. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was lost on this line.
111.5 is the time in minutes. The part asks for hours, and part (b) needs hours because the speed is in km/h.

parts.stem: Calculate the **greatest possible** average speed of the cyclist, in km/h.

scheme.for: 41.5 identified as the upper bound of the distance
41.5 divided by their shortest time in hours, or 41.5 × 60 ÷ 111.5

hints: Speed $=$ distance $\div$ time; it is not on the formula sheet.
Greatest speed: furthest distance in the shortest time.
parts.workedSolution: Distance: $40.5 \le d < 41.5$. Greatest average speed $= 41.5 \div 1.858333333\ldots = 22.331838565\ldots$ km/h. Equivalently $41.5 \times 60 \div 111.5$. The stored value is used, not $1.86$.

commonErrors.feedback: The time was rounded to 1.86 h before dividing. Keep the stored value: the scheme prints the long answer and rounding part-way moves the third figure.
$41 \div (112 \div 60)$ uses the given values, so it is the average speed itself and not a greatest possible value.

context.setting: A metal block weighed and measured in a workshop

parts.stem:
A metal block has a mass of $248$ g, correct to the nearest gram, and a volume of $92$ cm$^3$, correct to the nearest cm$^3$.

Write down the upper and lower bounds of the mass and of the volume.
hints: Nearest gram: half unit 0.5 g.
Nearest cm³: half unit 0.5 cm³.

parts.stem:
Density $=$ mass $\div$ volume.

Calculate the upper and lower bounds of the density of the block, in g/cm$^3$.

scheme.for: 2.715846995 and 2.675675676 (accept the full displays or 2.7158 and 2.6757)

hints: The largest density is the largest mass in the smallest volume.
The smallest density is the smallest mass in the largest volume.

commonErrors.feedback: $248.5 \div 92.5$ uses both upper bounds, so it is neither bound of the density. On the bottom of a fraction, the smallest value gives the largest result.

parts.stem:
Write down the density of the block to a **suitable degree of accuracy**.

Explain how your two bounds justify the accuracy you have chosen.

accepted: 2.7 g/cm3 because both bounds round to 2.7 to 2 significant figures, and to 3 significant figures they give 2.72 and 2.68, which disagree.
2.7 g/cm3; the bounds agree to 2 significant figures only.

scheme.for: reason: both bounds round to 2.7 to 2 significant figures, and they differ at 3 significant figures

hints: Round both bounds to 1, then 2, then 3 significant figures and watch where they stop agreeing.
Quote the last accuracy at which they still agree.
parts.workedSolution: To $2$ significant figures, $2.7158\ldots \to 2.7$ and $2.6757\ldots \to 2.7$: they agree. To $3$ significant figures they give $2.72$ and $2.68$: they disagree. So the density is $2.7$ g/cm$^3$, and no third figure can be claimed.

commonErrors.feedback: A third figure was quoted, or the midpoint of the bounds was given. Only the figures on which both bounds agree can be stated; here that stops at 2.7.

context.setting: Crates loaded onto a trailer at a builders' yard

parts.stem:
Each crate has a mass of $24$ kg, correct to the **nearest 2 kg**.

A trailer can carry a load of $700$ kg, correct to the **nearest 20 kg**.

Work out the **greatest possible number** of crates the trailer can carry.

Show your working clearly.

scheme.examinerNote: A maximum count is rounded down and must be a whole number.

hints: Half of 2 kg is 1 kg; half of 20 kg is 10 kg.
The most crates fit when the allowance is largest and each crate is lightest.
$710 \div 23 = 30.8695\ldots$, and a crate cannot be a fraction.
parts.workedSolution: Crate: $23 \le m < 25$. Trailer: $690 \le L < 710$. Greatest number $= 710 \div 23 = 30.869565\ldots$ Crates are whole, and $31$ crates would weigh at least $31 \times 23 = 713$ kg, which is above $710$ kg. So the greatest possible number is $30$.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole rounding units were added and subtracted: $720 \div 22$. Halve the rounding unit — 1 kg for the crate, 10 kg for the trailer. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 was decided on exactly this.
$30.87$ was rounded up. The 31st crate does not fit under any allowed load, so a greatest possible count is always rounded down; leaving 30.87 also loses the final mark.
$700 \div 24$ uses the given values. The bounds have to be written down before the division; those are the first two marks.

context.setting: A circle cut from a rectangular sheet of card

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 380 265' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Rectangular sheet of card 24.6 cm long and 18.3 cm wide with a circle of radius 5.4 cm cut from the middle'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'><rect x='58' y='34' width='260' height='193'/><circle cx='188' cy='130' r='57'/><path d='M188 130 L245 130' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/></g><circle cx='188' cy='130' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='currentColor'><text x='162' y='252'>24.6 cm</text><text x='2' y='136'>18.3 cm</text><text x='200' y='122'>5.4 cm</text><text x='58' y='22' font-size='12'>diagram not drawn accurately</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: A rectangular sheet of card, 24.6 cm long and 18.3 cm wide, with a circle of radius 5.4 cm removed from the middle. The radius is shown as a dashed line from the centre of the circle. Diagram not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
A circle of radius $5.4$ cm is cut from a rectangular sheet of card measuring $24.6$ cm by $18.3$ cm.

Each measurement is correct to $1$ decimal place.

Write down the three bounds needed to make the area of card left as large as possible.
hints: Every measurement has a half unit of 0.05.
A bigger rectangle leaves more card; a bigger hole leaves less.
parts.workedSolution: The rectangle takes both upper bounds, $24.65$ cm and $18.35$ cm, because a larger rectangle leaves more card. The circle takes its lower bound, $5.35$ cm, because a smaller hole removes less.

commonErrors.feedback: The circle was given its upper bound too. It is being removed, so the biggest area left needs the smallest possible circle.

parts.stem:
Calculate the **greatest possible** area of card left after the circle has been cut out.

Give your answer to $1$ decimal place.

scheme.for: their rectangle area - their circle area
362.4 (from 362.4072643); accept 362.41 or the full display only if 1 d.p. is also given

hints: Area of a circle is $\pi r^2$ and it is not on the formula sheet.
Use the stored value of $\pi$, not $3.14$.
parts.workedSolution: Rectangle: $24.65 \times 18.35 = 452.3275$ cm$^2$. Circle: $\pi \times 5.35^2 = 89.920235727\ldots$ cm$^2$. Greatest area left $= 452.3275 - 89.920235727\ldots = 362.407264272\ldots$, which is $362.4$ cm$^2$ to $1$ decimal place.

commonErrors.feedback: The given values were used: $24.6 \times 18.3 - \pi \times 5.4^2$. That is the area itself, not its greatest possible value. The first two marks are for the bounded areas.
$\pi$ was replaced by $3.14$, giving a circle area of $89.87465$ and a final answer of $362.5$. Use the calculator's $\pi$ and round once, at the end.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked: a sack of feed weighs $20$ kg, correct to the nearest $5$ kg; a store can hold $600$ kg, correct to the nearest $50$ kg. Work out the greatest possible number of sacks the store can hold. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The whole rounding unit was added and subtracted instead of half of it. Correct to the nearest 5 kg means the half unit is 2.5 kg, so the bounds are 17.5 kg and 22.5 kg. Line 2 has the same slip: half of 50 is 25, so the store bounds are 575 kg and 625 kg.
correction: Sack: 17.5 kg to 22.5 kg (half of 5 is 2.5)
Store: 575 kg to 625 kg (half of 50 is 25)
So 35 sacks, because 36 sacks would weigh at least 36 x 17.5 = 630 kg
findTheMistake.feedback: The structure is right: bounds first, then largest allowance divided by lightest sack, which is worth the method mark. Both bound lines use the whole rounding unit, and the last line then rounds a maximum count up. Halve the rounding unit, and round a greatest possible count down. Summer 2025 M4 Q13 lost most of its marks in exactly these two places.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin was asked: in a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $8.42$ cm, correct to $3$ significant figures, and one shorter side is $5.3$ cm, correct to $1$ decimal place. Using those bounds, calculate the upper bound of the third side. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The third side was calculated from the given values and the bound was added to the answer afterwards. Squaring and square-rooting change the size of a half unit, so a half unit added at the end means nothing. The bounds belong in line 1, and the correct pairing is the upper bound of the hypotenuse with the lower bound of the known side.
correction: Upper bound of the third side = sqrt(43.418125) = 6.589243128
findTheMistake.feedback: Pythagoras was set up correctly, but no mark is available until the bounds go in, so this scores nothing. Write the four bounds first, choose the upper hypotenuse with the lower side because that side is being taken away, then calculate once and leave the display. November 2025 M4 Q17: about 30% reached full marks, and bounding the answer instead of the inputs was the main reason.

findTheMistake.stem: Saoirse was asked: a runner covers $18$ km, correct to the nearest kilometre, in a time of $1$ hour $17$ minutes, correct to the nearest minute. Work out the greatest possible average speed, in km/h. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 1 hour 16.5 minutes was written as the decimal 1.165 hours. Minutes are sixtieths of an hour, not thousandths. The time should be turned into minutes first: 1 h 17 min is 77 minutes, so the minimum is 76.5 minutes, and 76.5 divided by 60 is 1.275 hours.
correction: 1 h 17 min = 77 minutes, so the minimum time is 76.5 minutes
Leave the full display unless an accuracy is stated
findTheMistake.feedback: The distance bound and the shape of the calculation are right, which earns the first method mark. The time conversion is the whole question: minutes divided by 60 gives decimal hours, and the error here moves the answer by about 1.4 km/h. Summer 2023 M4 Q15 was one of the least-answered questions on the paper for this reason, and rounding the final display to 15.9 would risk the accuracy mark as well.

prompts.prompt: The four moves for any bounds question.
prompts.answer: 1 Write the half unit for each quantity (half of the rounding unit). 2 Write all the bounds. 3 Choose the bound of each input that pushes the answer the way you want, and substitute once. 4 Leave the full calculator display, unless an accuracy is stated.

prompts.prompt: Greatest and least possible value of $a - b$?
Greatest and least possible value of $a \div b$?
A mass is $50$ kg to the nearest $5$ kg. What are its bounds, and why?
prompts.answer: $47.5$ kg and $52.5$ kg. The half unit is half of the rounding unit, and half of $5$ is $2.5$.

prompts.prompt: Half unit for: nearest 2, nearest 0.5, 1 decimal place, 2 significant figures in 3400?
prompts.answer: $1$; $0.25$; $0.05$; $50$. Always half of the place the accuracy names — for significant figures, half of the place value of the last significant figure.

prompts.prompt: A time is $1$ hour $11$ minutes to the nearest minute. How do you bound it for a speed in km/h?
prompts.answer: Change to minutes first: $71$ minutes, so the bounds are $70.5$ and $71.5$ minutes. Then divide by $60$: the shortest time is $70.5 \div 60 = 1.175$ h. Never write $1$ h $10.5$ min as $1.105$ h.

prompts.prompt: Why can you not calculate first and bound the answer afterwards?
prompts.answer: Because squaring, dividing and square-rooting all change the size of a half unit. The bounds belong to the inputs, so substitute them and calculate once.

prompts.prompt: A greatest possible number of whole items comes out as $28.46$. What goes on the answer line?
prompts.answer: $28$. A count of whole items is rounded down for a maximum, because the 29th item would not fit under any allowed load. A decimal on the answer line scores nothing.

prompts.prompt: For $h = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$, which bounds give the upper bound of $h$?
prompts.answer: Upper bound of $u$, squared, over twice the lower bound of $a$: $\dfrac{\text{UB}(u)^2}{2 \times \text{LB}(a)}$. $u$ is squared and $a$ is doubled.

prompts.prompt: The bounds of a length are $6.0473\ldots$ m and $6.0518\ldots$ m. How do you state it to a suitable degree of accuracy?
prompts.answer: Round both bounds to $1$, then $2$, then $3$ significant figures and stop at the last accuracy where they agree. Both give $6.05$ to $3$ significant figures; at $4$ they give $6.047$ and $6.052$, so the answer is $6.05$ m.

prompts.prompt: A display cuts off (truncates) at $1$ decimal place and shows $9.4$. What is the interval?
prompts.answer: $9.4 \le t < 9.5$. A truncated display is never above the true value, so the stated value is itself the lower bound.

prompts.prompt: When may you round a bound?
prompts.answer: Only when the question states an accuracy. Otherwise leave the full calculator display: the CCEA schemes print values such as $53.19148936$ and $3.863512003$, and the accuracy mark follows the display.

findings.asked: Use bounds of a distance and a time (in hours and minutes) to find a maximum average speed.
findings.wentWrong: A minority finished. The time bound was the obstacle: candidates bounded 70.5 minutes, or wrote 1 h 10.5 min as 1.105 h.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Converted the time to decimal hours, bounded it, then divided the upper distance by the lower time keeping the full display.
findings.rule: Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60 before finding bounds; max speed = max distance / min time.

findings.asked: Substitute bounds into a formula of the form v squared = u squared + 2as.
findings.wentWrong: Bounds were mostly identified. Errors were in the formula itself (u not squared, a not doubled); the weakest just substituted the given values.
findings.rule: Write the four bounds, then substitute the combination that maximises the target, using the formula exactly.

findings.asked: Bounds in a formula to find a maximum value.
findings.wentWrong: Improving year on year; the same formula slips (V not squared, g not doubled) and rounding errors at the end.
findings.rule: Read the formula symbol by symbol; keep the full display.

findings.asked: Maximum number of items given a total mass to the nearest 100 kg and an item mass to the nearest 5 kg.
findings.wentWrong: The nearest-5 bound was the problem: 45 was used instead of 47.5. Many did get the upper bound 1550. Some did not give a whole number, or rounded up when a maximum count must round down.
findings.rule: Half of 5 is 2.5; a maximum number of whole items is rounded down.

findings.wentWrong: About 30% got full marks. Many calculated with the given values and then bounded the answer; some used both upper bounds where the subtraction needed one upper and one lower; most rounded the result (3.86) instead of leaving the whole display.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Listed all four bounds, chose upper hypotenuse with lower leg for the maximum, and left the full display as the bound.
findings.rule: Bound the inputs, not the output; in a subtraction pair the biggest with the smallest.

insight.ruleToRemember: Write all four bounds first; subtraction and division mix an upper with a lower; convert units (minutes to decimal hours) before bounding; keep the full calculator display for a bound and round a maximum count down.
insight.aStarSignal: Bounds threaded through a two-stage calculation (a formula or Pythagoras, or a speed with a time in hours and minutes) with the right max/min pairing at each stage.
